vignette:
She is 33, European, married, and works as a graphic designer for a small branding agency. Before the stalking began, her life feels ordinary in the way she now misses deeply. She spends long days adjusting layouts, choosing colors, and refining logos until they feel balanced. She likes the control of visual work, the quiet logic of spacing and form. She and her husband have a familiar routine: dinner together when deadlines allow, a series in bed, weekend walks to the market. She does not think of herself as fearful. If anything, she is the person friends describe as composed.

The first contact seems small enough to dismiss. A man she does not know sends her a message through her professional portfolio site, complimenting her work with a tone that feels overly intimate. She ignores it. Then he writes again, this time mentioning the café where she had worked the previous afternoon. She remembers the jolt in her stomach as she rereads the sentence, trying to explain it away. Designers often post their locations; perhaps he has guessed. But over the next two weeks, the messages multiply. He comments on the coat she wore, on the groceries she carried, on how tired she looked one evening leaving the office. The details strip away her ability to pretend.

She blocks one account, then another, then another. He begins emailing her work address. Flowers arrive at the agency with no signature, then a printed card that includes a phrase she has only said once aloud to a colleague. After that, she starts scanning the street before leaving the office. She changes routes home, then changes them again. The city, once something she moves through absentmindedly, becomes a field of possible sightlines. Every slow-moving car makes her shoulders tighten. Every man lingering near the train platform pulls her attention like a magnet.

When she first sees him, she almost doubts herself. He is across the street from her building at dusk, not doing anything dramatic, only standing there as if waiting. But the stillness of him is what frightens her. She feels suddenly unable to fit the key into the front door. Later that night, she goes to the window over and over, part of her desperate to prove he is gone, part of her terrified she will find him. Her husband tries to reassure her, then becomes frightened himself when they discover fresh messages sent during the very hour she had been looking outside.

In the months that follow, her life narrows. At work, she is still productive, but only by exhausting herself. She closes the blinds near her desk because reflections in the glass make her heart race. She jumps when notifications appear on her screen and has to ask colleagues to forward client emails because opening her inbox fills her with dread. She once prides herself on presenting design concepts confidently, but now in meetings she loses her train of thought when she notices someone standing near the conference room door. Her manager gently suggests remote work for a while. She agrees, relieved and ashamed at once.

At home, sleep becomes fractured. She lies beside her husband listening for sounds in the hallway, replaying every encounter and every message, as if reviewing them closely enough might reveal how to make it stop. When she does fall asleep, she wakes abruptly, pulse hammering, from dreams in which she is being watched but cannot find from where. In the morning she feels foggy and irritable. She stops going to the market alone. She asks her husband to come downstairs when a package is delivered. If he is late coming home, she starts imagining stairwells, parking garages, all the places a body can be cornered.

What unsettles her most is the way fear settles inside ordinary things. She used to love observation, the designer's habit of noticing details others miss; now noticing feels dangerous. She studies faces on the street with painful intensity. She memorizes exits in cafés. She chooses clothing she thinks is less noticeable and then hates herself for thinking that way. Sometimes she becomes angry in a flash-at strangers who stand too close, at her husband for suggesting she rest, at herself for checking the lock three times and still not believing it.

The stalking eventually becomes less frequent after police involvement, but "less frequent" does not feel like "over." Even now, she measures each day against the possibility of reappearance. She keeps her social media empty, her portfolio stripped of personal details, her curtains closed earlier than she once did. When a new message arrives from an unknown sender, she feels her body react before her mind catches up: tight chest, cold hands, the old surge of alarm. She knows many people looking at her would not see any of this. They would see a woman on a video call discussing fonts and brand identity, a wife answering texts from her husband, a person carrying on. But inside, she is still living with the sense that someone could be just outside the frame, watching.
